clue.text: Ships' cooks, all in a row ?

definitions.text: Ships' cooks, all in a row ?

parts.words: Ships' cooks, all in a row
parts.note: the galley is a ship's kitchen, so its workers sound like cooks, but the men meant sat in rows pulling oars

explanation.surface: A ship's kitchen staff lined up neatly in a row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ships' cooks' suggests the galley as a kitchen; the rowers chained to the benches of an ancient galley are the real picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Convicts or captives forced to row the oared warships of antiquity were chained in rows on the benches.

indicators.note: moving erratically means the letters of the words around it are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: Someone dances wildly up to a gate numbered five.
explanation.walkthrough: 'erratically' scrambles TO, GATE and V (five in Roman numerals).
explanation.definitionFit: A gavotte is an old French court dance in moderate four-four time.

parts.note: worsted is a woollen suit cloth, but it also means beaten, the condition of someone who has been defeated

explanation.surface: A man who would look good in a woollen suit.
explanation.walkthrough: Worsted looks like the suiting fabric; read it as the past tense of worst, to defeat.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has been defeated in a contest has been worsted, beaten by a rival.

clue.text: It's persuasive, in a manner of speaking

definitions.text: It's persuasive, in a manner of speaking

parts.words: It's persuasive, in a manner of speaking
parts.note: 'in a manner of speaking' looks like the idiom for 'so to speak' but literally describes a fluent, moving way of talking

explanation.surface: A hedging remark that something is sort of persuasive.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'in a manner of speaking' usually means 'loosely', but here it is literal: a manner of speaking that persuades.
explanation.definitionFit: Fluent, forceful and persuasive speech or writing is the quality of an accomplished orator.

clue.text: Money in raising North Sea wealth? Dross

indicators.note: the money abbreviation is placed inside the reversed fuel word
in a down clue, raising a word means writing it from the bottom up, so it reads backwards

parts.note: natural gas from under the North Sea made Britain rich
L is the abbreviation for pounds, the British currency

explanation.surface: Is the money from North Sea fuel really just rubbish?
explanation.walkthrough: 'raising' turns GAS into SAG; 'in' puts L (pounds, from the Latin libra) inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Slag is the waste matter left after smelting ore, worthless refuse.

clue.text: Location immaterial — ditto clothes, some say

indicators.note: what some people say out loud signals a word that sounds like the phrase built

parts.note: ditto repeats 'immaterial', so 'any' clothes, any wear

explanation.surface: A remark that it doesn't matter where you go, nor what you wear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ditto' repeats the idea of 'immaterial' (any), and clothes are WEAR; spoken, ANY WEAR matches the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: If the place does not matter, any place at all will do.

clue.text: I care madly for Miss Heath

indicators.note: acting madly means the letters of the preceding words are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A suitor declares wild devotion to a woman called Miss Heath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss Heath' reads as a woman's name; it is a girl's name that is also the botanical name of heath plants.
explanation.definitionFit: Erica is the genus of heaths and heathers, and also a woman's first name, so a 'Miss' who is a heath.

parts.note: a garden plant food made of ground bones, which sounds like a dinner for a dog but would not feed one

explanation.surface: Plant food for the garden that is no use as dog food.
explanation.walkthrough: Fido is a stock name for a dog and Flora stands for plants; ground bones feed plants, though a dog would expect bones as a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Crushed animal bones are sold as a slow-release garden fertiliser rich in phosphate.

clue.text: Island might lose one leader of Persia to another

definitions.text: Island might lose one leader of Persia to another

parts.words: Island might lose one leader of Persia to another
parts.note: take away the first letter of Persia from the island's name and what remains is the name of a famous Persian king

explanation.surface: An island nation fears being taken over by a succession of Persian rulers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one leader of Persia' is P, the first letter; without it the island becomes CYRUS, the great Persian king, 'another' leader of Persia.
explanation.definitionFit: Cyprus is a large island in the eastern Mediterranean.

parts.note: a famous line from Wordsworth's ode on intimations of immortality with one adjective left blank to be filled in

explanation.surface: A quotation from Wordsworth with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The line from Wordsworth's Intimations Ode reads 'Whither is fled the ___ gleam?'; supply the missing adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet laments the lost dreamlike, imaginative radiance that he saw in nature as a child.

definitions.meaning: made of or like the metal iron, iron-ish
Socrates feigned ignorance to draw out his pupils, a rhetorical technique of saying the opposite of what one means

explanation.surface: A metal gadget used by the Greek philosopher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ferrous device' looks like an iron tool; split it into an adjective meaning iron-like and Socratic pretended ignorance.
explanation.definitionFit: The word can mean 'containing iron', and Socrates' feigned ignorance is the classic rhetorical dissembling.

clue.text: The moment for doing a good turn

definitions.text: The moment for doing a good turn

parts.words: The moment for doing a good turn
parts.note: the time for a kind deed, but in physics a moment is a turning force

explanation.surface: The right time to do someone a favour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moment' and 'good turn' suggest timing and kindness; in mechanics the moment of a force about an axis is what makes it turn.
explanation.definitionFit: In physics it is the turning force on a shaft or axle, measured as a moment.

parts.note: a small songbird whose name splits into the grain spike that flour is milled from

explanation.surface: Naming the bird that provides our daily bread.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird's name splits into two words: the spike of grain from which bread flour comes.
explanation.definitionFit: A small migratory songbird of open country, whose name also describes a head of cereal grain.

clue.text: The little beast's in a determined mood

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the word that follows, so the answer lies within it

explanation.surface: A small animal is in a stubborn frame of mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'determined mood' suggests resolve; the creature is in the letters of 'determined'.
explanation.definitionFit: A stoat, a small carnivorous mammal, is called this when in its white winter coat.

clue.text: Eastern official of the Orange Order ?

definitions.meaning: a senior civil servant of imperial China
a member of the citrus family, a small loose-skinned orange, not of the Protestant Orange Order

explanation.surface: A Chinese bureaucrat who belongs to the Orange Order.
explanation.walkthrough: The Orange Order is a Protestant fraternity in Northern Ireland; here 'Orange order' just means the orange kind of fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both an imperial Chinese bureaucrat and a small, easily peeled citrus fruit.

parts.note: ophidian means snake-like, and snakes move along the ground as some climbing or trailing plants do

explanation.surface: Asking for plants that resemble snakes.
explanation.walkthrough: Ophidian means relating to snakes; plants that trail or climb share the snake's way of moving.
explanation.definitionFit: Plants that trail along the ground or climb walls are named for their slow, snake-like spread.

parts.note: Shakespeare's prince asks 'To be, or not to be', doubting whether being alive is worthwhile

explanation.surface: The Danish prince challenged something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To be, or not to be: that is the question' puts being itself in doubt.
explanation.definitionFit: Being alive, the state of being, is what Hamlet's famous soliloquy questions.

parts.note: in Genesis the first woman was made from a rib taken from the first man, and a cut of pork ribs is a dish

explanation.surface: Eve, described as Adam's own dish.
explanation.walkthrough: Eve was formed from one of Adam's ribs, one he could spare; the same words name a pork dish, and 'dish' is also slang for an attractive woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A cut of pork ribs with most of the meat trimmed off is a familiar dish, and Eve came from Adam's surplus rib.

clue.text: It's very low-down to be beneath it

definitions.text: It's very low-down to be beneath it

parts.words: It's very low-down to be beneath it
parts.note: behaviour described as beneath something deserves only scorn, the idiom of utter disdain

explanation.surface: A remark that something is very base behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom is 'beneath contempt': anything below it is low indeed.
explanation.definitionFit: Utter scorn or disdain; something so base as to be below even scorn is very low.

clue.text: Vulgar fellow in transatlantic intelligence — chirpy type

indicators.note: the rough fellow is placed inside the intelligence agency

parts.note: the CIA is the American intelligence agency, across the Atlantic from Britain
a cad is an ill-mannered man

explanation.surface: A coarse man works in American intelligence and is a cheery sort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chirpy type' looks like a cheerful person; it is an insect that chirps.
explanation.definitionFit: This insect is known for the loud shrill chirping song the males make in summer.

parts.note: sounds like bridle paths for horse riders, but means the passages a bride walks along in church

explanation.surface: Tracks for riding horses.
explanation.walkthrough: A bridle path is for horses; a bride walks up the passage between church pews.
explanation.definitionFit: The passages between rows of pews in a church are where a bride walks to the altar.

parts.note: Neptune is the sea god and weed is slang for tobacco, so the sea god's tobacco is ocean plant life

explanation.surface: The sea god's tobacco.
explanation.walkthrough: Baccy is British slang for tobacco, which is also called 'weed'; Neptune rules the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Marine algae such as kelp and wrack grow in the sea, and tobacco is jokingly called weed.

definitions.meaning: ships that trade along a coastline
small mats or trays on which a wine bottle or glass is set

explanation.surface: Ships occasionally carrying a cargo of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessels carrying wine' looks like one picture; split it into ships and table mats that hold decanters.
explanation.definitionFit: Small trading ships hug the coast, and the same word means mats or stands for bottles and glasses.

clue.text: If they start to go they can be stopped

definitions.text: If they start to go they can be stopped

parts.words: If they start to go they can be stopped
parts.note: decaying molars can be filled, and a filling is also called a stopping

explanation.surface: Something that can be halted once it begins to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stopped' means filled, as a dentist stops a cavity; 'go' means decay.
explanation.definitionFit: When molars begin to decay a dentist can fill, or stop, the cavities.

parts.note: Jonathan Swift wrote a famous series of letters to a woman he called by a pet name

explanation.surface: A woman who writes letters quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swift' is Jonathan Swift, author of Gulliver's Travels, whose letters to Esther Johnson were published as the Journal to Stella.
explanation.definitionFit: Esther Johnson, Jonathan Swift's close friend, received his letters under this name.

parts.note: Tours is a French city on a great river, though the word looks like boat trips

explanation.surface: Boat trips run on this river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tours' looks like excursions; it is the French city standing on this river.
explanation.definitionFit: France's longest river flows through the Touraine past the city of Tours and its chateaux.

definitions.meaning: a Mac is a stock name for a Scotsman, from the common surname prefix
an old word for a levy or payment

explanation.surface: A tax on Scotsmen.
explanation.walkthrough: Scot as a tax survives in 'scot-free', meaning without paying.
explanation.definitionFit: A Mac is a Scotsman by nickname, and a municipal levy was once called a scot.

clue.text: Impulse needed to start a round, of course

definitions.meaning: an inner urge or motivating force

definitions.text: needed to start a round, of course
definitions.meaning: on a golf course the first stroke from each tee

explanation.surface: Motivation needed to begin a round, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' looks like 'naturally' but means on a golf course, where the tee shot starts each hole.
explanation.definitionFit: An urge or determination, and the long opening shot in golf, share the same word.

indicators.note: an arrangement of the preceding words means their letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Something that was once tested is now an unusual setup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arrangement' rearranges ONCE TRIED.
explanation.definitionFit: Recondite knowledge is obscure, little known and remote from ordinary understanding.

clue.text: Somewhat ropy for Jack when the pub runs out of beer

definitions.meaning: Jack is a sailor, and to sailors this means the last part of a rope or anchor cable

definitions.text: when the pub runs out of beer
definitions.meaning: bitter is a British beer, so its end comes when it is all drunk

explanation.surface: A sailor is somewhat poorly when his pub runs dry.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack (Jack Tar) means a sailor; bitter is a British pale ale. 'ropy' means poorly in British slang but here means rope-related.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors use the phrase for the inboard end of a rope, and its usual sense is the very last point.
